add_trace.summary: Adds a graph-object trace or trace dictionary to a Plotly figure. Subplot coordinates and secondary-axis options can control where the trace is placed.
add_trace.explanation: `add_trace` accepts a graph-object trace or a trace dictionary and appends it to a figure. For figures made with `make_subplots`, `row` and `col` select the destination subplot; the method returns the figure so calls can be chained.

parameters.name: trace
parameters.description: Trace object or dictionary to add. A dictionary uses `type` to identify the trace type; without it, scatter is assumed.

parameters.name: row
parameters.description: One-based subplot row index; `all` addresses all rows in selected columns. Valid for subplot figures.

parameters.name: col
parameters.description: One-based subplot column index; `all` addresses all columns in selected rows. Valid for subplot figures.

parameters.name: secondary_y
parameters.description: Whether to place the trace on the secondary y-axis.

parameters.name: exclude_empty_subplots
parameters.description: When true, do not add the trace to subplots that do not already contain traces.

add_trace.returns: The figure on which `add_trace` was called; return type BaseFigure.

example.title: Add traces to subplots
example.code:
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(y=[4, 2, 1], mode="lines"), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(y=[2, 1, 3]), row=1, col=2)
fig.show()

interview.question: What does `Figure.add_trace` accept and return?
interview.answer: `add_trace` adds one graph-object trace, such as `go.Scatter` or `go.Bar`, to a figure and returns the figure. A trace dictionary is also accepted.
interview.followUp: How would you target a subplot? Create the figure with `make_subplots`, then pass its one-based `row` and `col` values to `add_trace`.

interview.question: How are dictionary traces interpreted?
interview.answer: A trace dictionary must identify its trace kind with the `type` property, for example `scatter` or `bar`. If `type` is omitted, Plotly assumes `scatter`.
interview.followUp: Why might using a graph-object constructor be preferable? It makes the trace class explicit and supplies its typed properties directly.

callback.explanation: This method registers a callable for point-click events on a trace. The handler receives the trace, a Points object containing selected indices, and an InputDeviceState object; setting append=True preserves existing handlers instead of replacing them.

example.title: Handle point clicks
example.code:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.FigureWidget([go.Scatter(x=[1, 2], y=[3, 0])])

def click_fn(trace, points, state):
    print(points.point_inds)

fig.data[0].on_click(click_fn)

interview.followUp: How would you preserve an existing handler? Pass append=True when registering the new callback.

interview.followUp: What is the practical consequence of omitting append when composing handlers? Earlier handlers are removed for that trace.

interview.question: What does fig.update_xaxes do?

interview.question: What does `fig.write_html` do?

interview.followUp: How would you avoid generating a complete document? Set `full_html=False` so the output contains only the figure code needed by a surrounding template.

interview.question: What is `pio.templates` used for?
interview.answer: `pio.templates` is the configuration object for registered Plotly themes. It exposes available templates and supports changing the default through its `default` property.
interview.followUp: How would you inspect the available choices? Evaluate `pio.templates` or iterate over it with `list(pio.templates)`, which returns registered names.

interview.question: How do you change the default template?
interview.answer: Set `pio.templates.default` to a registered template name, such as `"plotly_white"`. New Plotly Express or graph-object figures without an explicit theme then use that default.
interview.followUp: How can one disable theming globally? Set `pio.templates.default = "none"`.

interview.question: How do you register a custom template?
interview.answer: A template can be registered by assigning a template object to a name in `pio.templates`, for example `pio.templates["draft"] = custom_template`. That name can then be used as a figure template or as the default.
interview.followUp: What can a figure's template value be besides a registered name? It can also be a `Template` object or a dictionary accepted by the constructor.

interview.question: What does px.box produce and what do its boxes represent?
interview.answer: px.box returns a Plotly Figure. It groups data-frame rows into box-and-whisker marks; each box covers Q1 through Q3 and the median is shown inside it.

interview.question: How do you control the points displayed over a box plot?
interview.answer: The points argument controls raw observations: "all" displays every point, "outliers" displays only outliers, and False hides them. The default is outliers.
interview.followUp: What does notched=True change? It requests notched boxes, which provide a visual indication related to uncertainty around the median.

interview.followUp: How would you map US states? Use state identifiers with `locationmode='USA-states'` and typically set `scope='usa'` for the geographic view.

interview.followUp: What must be true for custom GeoJSON data to work? Each GeoJSON feature needs an identifier, or an identifying value in its properties, that matches the values used in `locations`.

interview.question: What does `px.density_contour` calculate?
interview.answer: It groups observations into two-dimensional x/y bins and uses the resulting aggregate to draw contour levels. With no `z`, the default aggregate is a count; with `z`, `histfunc` can define an operation such as `avg`.
interview.followUp: How would you visualize dense data without plotting every point? Use a density contour or density heatmap to aggregate overlapping observations into bins.

interview.question: What input shapes can the function accept?
interview.answer: Pass a dataframe as the first argument and identify the plotted columns with `x` and `y`. For wide-form data, the 2D-Cartesian Plotly Express functions, including `density_contour`, can also accept wide or mixed input.
interview.followUp: What dependency is relevant when passing a dictionary or array as `data_frame`? Plotly Express internally converts it to a pandas DataFrame, so pandas must be installed.

interview.question: How can a density contour represent values other than counts?
interview.answer: Use `z` to provide values for aggregation and `histfunc` to choose the aggregation operation. For example, `z="sepal_length"` with `histfunc="avg"` makes each bin represent the average z value rather than a row count.
interview.followUp: How can the displayed contour appearance be changed after creation? Update the generated trace, for example with `fig.update_traces(contours_coloring="fill", contours_showlabels=True)`.

interview.question: What does `px.strip` visualize?
interview.answer: `px.strip` produces a strip chart: individual points are shown without the box or violin body. It is useful for displaying the distribution of observations across categories.
interview.followUp: How can it accept multiple data layouts? It accepts long-form data and also supports wide-form and mixed-form input as a 2D Cartesian Plotly Express function.

interview.question: How are data and columns supplied to `px.strip`?
interview.answer: The first positional argument is `data_frame`. Columns can then be supplied by name through arguments such as `x`, `y`, and `color`.
interview.followUp: What is a wide-form call? Pass a list of data-frame column names, such as `y=["a", "b"]`, to trigger wide-form processing.

interview.question: What does the function return?
interview.answer: It returns a Plotly figure generated from the supplied data and encoding options. The figure can be displayed with `fig.show()` and further configured with Plotly figure methods.
interview.followUp: How would you add grouping? Supply a grouping encoding such as `color`, then customize the returned figure or traces as needed.

keyPoints: The chart emphasizes every observation rather than summarizing the distribution with a visible box.
Long-form data is directly supported, with columns mapped to the chart through named arguments.
Because it is a 2D Cartesian function, `px.strip` also accepts wide-form and mixed-form inputs.
`px.strip` belongs to Plotly Express's group of functions with wide-form and mixed-form support.
gotchas: Pass the data frame first, then refer to its columns by name in arguments such as `x`, `y`, and `color`.

px.sunburst.explanation: Call px.sunburst with tabular data and either path columns or explicit ids and parents. The path form derives the hierarchy from successive columns; values controls sector sizing, while color can encode an additional measure. The function returns a Plotly Figure that can be displayed or further customized.

interview.question: How does px.sunburst represent hierarchical tabular data?
interview.answer: Use path when each hierarchy level is stored in its own DataFrame column. Each row contributes to the resulting sunburst hierarchy, and values can determine sector size.
interview.followUp: When would explicit ids and parents be preferable? They are useful when the hierarchy is already represented as node identifiers and parent relationships rather than rectangular level columns.

interview.question: How is a root node represented with explicit parents?
interview.answer: The parents representation assigns each sector a parent; the root uses an empty string as its parent. This directly describes the tree structure.
interview.followUp: What constraint applies when path is supplied? id and parent should not also be provided.

interview.question: How does numeric color aggregation work?
interview.answer: A color argument adds a measure or category used for node coloring. For a numeric measure, a node’s color is computed from its children using a value-weighted average.
interview.followUp: What determines the weighting? The child sectors’ values provide the weights, so the aggregation reflects their sizes.

keyPoints: The chart displays a hierarchy as concentric sectors extending from a root node toward leaf nodes.
Rows in the input DataFrame contribute sectors to the generated visualization.
Use path with an ordered list of columns to define hierarchy levels.
In an explicit parent-based hierarchy, assign the root an empty-string parent.
Numeric node colors aggregate child colors using the children’s values as weights.
gotchas: Do not combine path with id or parent; choose either the column-based hierarchy or the explicit parent-child representation.
For uneven hierarchy rows, represent absent levels with None so the hierarchy remains valid.

px.timeline.summary: px.timeline creates a Plotly timeline in which each data-frame row becomes a horizontal bar spanning start and end dates. It returns a figure with a date x-axis by default and supports categorical or continuous color mapping.
px.timeline.explanation: px.timeline converts rows in a data frame into horizontal duration bars. Map the start and end columns with x_start and x_end, choose the category axis with y, and optionally map color to another column; the resulting figure uses a date x-axis by default.

parameters.name: data_frame
parameters.description: Data frame containing the plotted columns; the reference signature abbreviates the remaining arguments after the initial parameters.

parameters.name: x_start
parameters.description: Column or array supplying each bar's start date or time.

parameters.name: x_end
parameters.description: Column or array supplying each bar's end date or time.

parameters.name: y
parameters.description: Column or array defining the categorical y-axis positions.

px.timeline.returns: A Plotly figure representing the timeline.

example.title: Basic project timeline
example.code:
import pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px

df = pd.DataFrame([
    {"Task": "Design", "Start": "2025-01-01", "Finish": "2025-01-10"},
    {"Task": "Build", "Start": "2025-01-06", "Finish": "2025-01-20"},
])
fig = px.timeline(df, x_start="Start", x_end="Finish", y="Task")
fig.update_yaxes(autorange="reversed")
fig.show()
example.explanation: Creates a timeline in which each task is displayed as a horizontal bar spanning its start and finish dates.

interview.question: What does px.timeline represent?
interview.answer: It creates a Plotly figure where every data-frame row becomes a horizontal rectangular bar. The bar begins at x_start and ends at x_end, while y identifies the task or category.
interview.followUp: How would you show ownership? Map a resource column to color, for example color="Resource", so the bars receive a discrete color category.

interview.question: Which arguments are required for a basic timeline?
interview.answer: Use x_start and x_end to provide the start and finish fields, and y to provide the task field. A minimal call is px.timeline(df, x_start="Start", x_end="Finish", y="Task").
interview.followUp: What axis type should be expected? The function defaults the x-axis to date, allowing date-axis configuration such as other time-series charts.

interview.question: When was px.timeline introduced, and what problem does it address?
interview.answer: The function was introduced in Plotly version 4.9. It is the recommended Plotly Express approach for timeline or Gantt-style charts in the supplied documentation.
interview.followUp: What legacy alternative appears in the documentation? The figure-factory create_gantt function is listed as an older option, with px.timeline recommended instead.

keyPoints: px.timeline was introduced in Plotly 4.9 for constructing timeline and Gantt-style visualizations.
Each row becomes a horizontal duration bar whose endpoints come from date-valued start and finish fields.
The x-axis is configured as a date axis by default, making temporal formatting and range controls applicable.
Color can encode either discrete categories or a continuous numeric measure, depending on the mapped data.
gotchas: Reverse the y-axis when you want the first task listed at the top; the default categorical ordering places tasks from the bottom upward.
Expect date-axis behavior by default, so date strings or datetime values are interpreted along a temporal x-axis.

interview.question: What does px.treemap produce, and how can a hierarchy be specified?
interview.answer: The function returns a Plotly figure representing hierarchical data as nested rectangles. With explicit data, names define node labels and parents define each node’s parent.
interview.followUp: How would you build the hierarchy from dataframe columns? Pass the columns in order through path, rather than constructing names and parents manually.

interview.question: How does path simplify treemaps from tabular data?
interview.answer: Each dataframe row becomes a treemap sector when using px.treemap. The path argument maps successive dataframe columns to hierarchy levels, while values determines the quantitative sizing of sectors.
interview.followUp: What restriction applies to path? Do not also provide id or parent when path is used.

interview.question: How is color aggregated in a hierarchical treemap?
interview.answer: When color is supplied, a node’s color is calculated from its children as a value-weighted average of their color values. This lets color summarize a metric across the hierarchy rather than merely label categories.
interview.followUp: What data-quality precaution improves the result? Ensure the first path element is a single root node.

keyPoints: The chart represents hierarchy through nested rectangular sectors.
Dataframe rows are converted into treemap sectors.
Use path with an ordered list of dataframe columns to derive hierarchy levels.
Color summarizes children using a value-weighted average.
Selecting a sector supports zooming and reveals the navigation pathbar.
gotchas: Do not combine path with id or parent inputs.
A path hierarchy works best when its first element identifies one root node.
Use None for absent levels in an irregular rectangular dataset.

px.violin.summary: Creates an interactive violin plot for visualizing numerical-data distributions. It supports categorical comparisons, box plots, and optional observation points.
px.violin.explanation: `px.violin` builds an interactive statistical distribution chart from a dataframe. Map a numeric column to `y` or `x`, optionally split distributions with a categorical dimension such as `color`, and use options such as `box` and `points` to add complementary distribution details.
px.violin.syntax: plotly.express.violin(data_frame=None, x=None, y=None, color=None, ..., box=False, points=None, violinmode=None, **kwargs)

parameters.name: data_frame
parameters.description: Dataframe or compatible data source containing the columns used by the chart.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Column or columns supplying the horizontal coordinate or categorical grouping.

parameters.name: y
parameters.description: Column or columns supplying the numerical values.

parameters.name: color
parameters.description: Column used to split observations into colored distributions.

parameters.name: box
parameters.description: Whether to draw a box plot inside each violin.

parameters.name: points
parameters.description: Which observations to display as points: `all`, `outliers`, or `False`.

example.title: Grouped violin plot
example.code:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.tips()
fig = px.violin(
    df,
    x="day",
    y="total_bill",
    color="sex",
    box=True,
    points="all",
)
fig.show()
example.explanation: Creates an interactive violin chart of total bills by day, splitting distributions by sex and displaying both an inner box plot and all observations.

interview.question: What does `px.violin` visualize?
interview.answer: It creates a violin plot, which combines a distribution shape with statistical information similar to a box plot. The chart is returned as a Plotly figure and can be rendered with `fig.show()`.
interview.followUp: How would you show individual observations? Pass `points="all"`, or use `points="outliers"` to limit markers to outliers.

interview.question: How do you compare distributions across categories?
interview.answer: Use `x` and `y` to map dataframe columns to the chart axes. Add `color` to create separate distributions by category, and `box=True` to draw a box plot inside each violin.
interview.followUp: How can several category violins be arranged? Use `violinmode="group"` for side-by-side violins or `violinmode="overlay"` to place them over one another.

interview.question: What dataframe shapes can the function handle?
interview.answer: The function accepts long-form data and also supports wide-form and mixed-form data. In wide form, a list of dataframe columns can be supplied, such as `y=["experiment_1", "experiment_2"]`.
interview.followUp: What alternative is available when Plotly Express is not sufficient? Use the more generic `plotly.graph_objects.Violin` class for lower-level trace control.

keyPoints: Use it to show the distribution of numerical observations rather than only a single summary statistic.
Compared with a box plot, the violin shape exposes the estimated density and distribution form.
Long-form data is supported as the general input style for Plotly Express functions.
`px.violin` also accepts wide-form and mixed-form data, including multiple dataframe columns.
Pass the source dataframe as the first positional argument, or provide it with the `data_frame` keyword.
For advanced trace-level customization, the related `go.Violin` class provides the lower-level interface.
gotchas: With wide-form data, Plotly Express automatically assigns the variable names to `x` and the dataframe columns to `y`; specify axes explicitly when that default is not desired.
The `points` option accepts `all`, `outliers`, or `False`; choose deliberately because displaying every observation can make dense distributions difficult to read.

update_layout.summary: Updates a Plotly figure's layout from a dictionary, keyword arguments, or both. Updates are recursive by default and the Figure object is returned.
update_layout.explanation: Call update_layout on a Figure to change layout properties using either a dictionary, keyword arguments, or both. Nested dictionaries are merged recursively by default; set overwrite=True when the supplied values should replace existing nested properties.

parameters.name: dict1
parameters.description: Dictionary of layout properties to update.

parameters.name: overwrite
parameters.description: If True, overwrite existing properties; otherwise apply recursive updates while preserving unspecified properties.

parameters.name: kwargs
parameters.description: Keyword/value pairs of layout properties to update.

update_layout.returns: The Figure object that update_layout was called on; return type BaseFigure.

example.title: Update a figure layout
example.code:
import plotly.express as px

fig = px.scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[3, 1, 2])
fig.update_layout(
    title="Sample chart",
    width=600,
    height=400,
    margin=dict(l=40, r=20, t=60, b=40),
)
fig.show()
example.explanation: Creates a scatter figure, then changes several layout properties with keyword arguments and a nested margin dictionary.

interview.question: What does Figure.update_layout do, and what does it return?
interview.answer: update_layout changes a figure's layout using a dictionary, keyword arguments, or both. It returns the same Figure object, so calls can be chained or followed by other figure operations.
interview.followUp: How can nested properties be replaced rather than merged? Pass overwrite=True to replace existing properties instead of recursively applying the update.

interview.question: How are nested layout dictionaries handled by default?
interview.answer: The method recursively updates the existing layout structure by default. For example, supplying margin=dict(t=60) changes the top margin while preserving other existing margin values.
interview.followUp: What happens if overwrite=True is supplied? Existing nested properties are overwritten by the supplied update rather than preserved when omitted.

interview.question: What inputs can update_layout accept?
interview.answer: The signature accepts dict1=None, overwrite=False, and arbitrary keyword arguments. dict1 contains properties to update, while kwargs provide property/value pairs such as title or width.
interview.followUp: Can the dictionary and keyword forms be combined? Yes; both are accepted in the same call and contribute to the layout update.

keyPoints: Use a mapping, keyword arguments, or both to specify layout changes.
Nested layout values are merged into the existing layout rather than rebuilding the whole layout by default.
Set overwrite=True when the incoming layout should replace existing properties.
The method returns the Figure instance on which it was invoked.
Keyword arguments represent individual layout property/value updates.
gotchas: The default recursive behavior preserves unspecified nested layout properties; use overwrite=True only when replacement is intended.
